description: A first college course: programming in Python, and how computers, networks and data work.

sets.title: What Is Computing?
sets.description: What computing is: algorithms, pseudocode and flowcharts, tracing simple programs, the history of computing hardware, and using AI assistants responsibly.

intro.story: The Recursive Dragon has scattered the Guild's founding scrolls — the ones that explain what computing actually IS — through the entrance halls of its labyrinth. Ada the Artificer, the Guild's mentor, waits inside to show you her tricks of the trade.
objectives: Explain what an algorithm is, and why the idea matters more than any machine
Read pseudocode and flowcharts, and trace short programs by hand
Follow the story of computing hardware from gears and punch cards to integrated circuits
Use AI assistants responsibly — and verify their work before trusting it

sets.title: Machine Architecture
sets.description: How machines compute: transistors and logic gates, the von Neumann architecture and fetch-decode-execute, the memory hierarchy and caching, binary/hex/two's-complement, and how text, images, and sound become numbers.

intro.story: Deeper in, the walls tick like clockwork. This wing holds the Dragon's machinery: the switches, circuits, and number systems every computer is built from. Ada has pried open the panels so you can watch the heartbeat inside.
objectives: Explain how transistors and logic gates carry out computation
Describe the von Neumann architecture and the fetch-decode-execute cycle
Rank the memory hierarchy and explain why caching makes programs fast
Convert between binary, decimal, and hexadecimal by hand
Explain two's complement, integer overflow, and how text, images, and sound become numbers

sets.title: Python Basics
sets.description: First Python: variables and the four core data types, arithmetic/comparison/boolean operators and precedence, f-strings and string methods, type casting and input, and tracing short programs by hand.

intro.story: Beyond the machinery lies a chamber of glowing runes — real Python, the language the Guild uses to command machines. Ada insists you learn to read the runes the way the machine does before you write your own.
objectives: Create variables and identify the four core data types
Evaluate arithmetic, comparison, and boolean expressions using operator precedence
Build output with f-strings and transform text with string methods
Convert between types and handle user input safely
Trace short programs by hand, line by line

sets.title: Control Flow & Functions
sets.description: if/elif/else and nested decisions, and/or/not with short-circuiting, while/for loops with range, break/continue and infinite loops, and functions with parameters, defaults, return values, keyword arguments, and scope.

intro.story: Past the rune chamber the corridor forks, and forks again. This is the gatehouse: doors that open only on a condition, stairs that loop back on themselves, and levers that do a whole job at one pull. Ada is waiting at the first fork with a piece of chalk.
objectives: Write and trace if / elif / else decisions, including nested ones
Combine conditions with and, or, and not, and explain short-circuiting
Count the passes of while and for loops, and use break and continue
Define functions with parameters, defaults, and return values
Explain why a variable made inside a function is invisible outside it

sets.title: Collections & ADTs
sets.description: Lists, tuples, dictionaries and sets: choosing the right one, indexing and slicing, the aliasing trap, nested list-of-dict data, comprehensions, and abstract data types.

intro.story: The vaults below hold everything the Guild has ever gathered — some shelved in order, some sorted by label, some sealed against change. Learning which container to reach for is most of the work down here. So is learning when two labels hang on the same chest.
objectives: Choose between a list, tuple, dictionary, and set for a given job
Index and slice sequences, and look up dictionary keys safely
Recognise the aliasing trap and make genuinely independent copies
Work with nested data such as a list of dictionaries
Read list comprehensions, and explain what an abstract data type separates

sets.title: Modules & Objects
sets.description: Imports and the standard library, then classes and objects: __init__, self, methods, inheritance and super(), polymorphism, composition, and designing with cohesion and coupling.

intro.story: Ada's own workshop, at last. Shelves of ready-made tools line one wall — the standard library, free for the taking. Along the other wall stand clay golems in various states of completion, each one built from a design she wrote herself. Today you write a design.
objectives: Import and use modules from the standard library
Define classes with __init__, attributes, and methods, and write methods that use self correctly
Build subclasses with inheritance, super(), and overridden methods
Explain encapsulation, polymorphism, and abstraction
Choose between inheritance and composition, and judge cohesion and coupling

sets.title: Searching, Sorting & Big-O
sets.description: Linear and binary search, selection and merge sort, sorted() with key=, reasoning about growth with Big-O, and the limits of computation: Turing machines, the halting problem, and P vs NP.

intro.story: The Guild library runs deeper than the torchlight reaches. Anything can be found here, if you know how to look — and some things cannot be found at all, no matter how long you search. At the very bottom is a door that no algorithm has ever opened.
objectives: Trace linear search and binary search, and say when each applies
Walk through selection sort and merge sort, and compare their costs
Reason about growth with Big-O and rank the common classes
Sort with sorted() and .sort(), including a key function
Explain the halting problem, undecidability, and what P vs NP asks

sets.title: Software Engineering
sets.description: The software development life cycle, waterfall versus agile, requirements and user stories, git and code review, testing with assert, and reviewing AI-written code responsibly.

intro.story: One apprentice with a good idea is not a Guild. The hall above the workshop is where crews plan, split, and ship work that no single person could hold in their head — and where every change is written into a bound history that never forgets who did what.
objectives: Compare waterfall and agile, and name the stages of the SDLC
Write requirements as user stories and plan work in sprints
Use git to stage, commit, branch, and share work through pull requests
Explain what tests and code review protect against over a project's life
Work responsibly with an AI assistant, treating the spec as the real artifact

sets.title: Databases & the Relational Model
sets.description: Why applications use databases, the relational model (tables, rows, columns, primary and foreign keys), basic SQL (CREATE, INSERT, SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, JOIN, GROUP BY), integrity constraints, and relational vs. document stores.

intro.story: The archive is the oldest room in the labyrinth, and the strictest. Every fact is written exactly once, in exactly one place, and the archivist will refuse an entry that breaks the rules rather than let a contradiction in. Ada says the refusals are the point.
objectives: Explain why databases beat flat files, and what tables, rows, and columns are
Use primary and foreign keys to connect tables
Query with SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, and ORDER BY
Insert, update, and delete data, and tell DDL from DML
Describe integrity constraints and when a document database fits better

sets.title: OS, Networks, Cloud & the Web
sets.description: OS responsibilities (processes, files, memory), how a request crosses the internet (IP, DNS, packets, TCP, the four-layer model), HTTP requests/responses/status codes, calling APIs with Python requests and JSON, cloud models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS), and Flask routes and templates.

intro.story: Up on the ramparts you can finally see out. Messages leave the labyrinth in numbered packets, cross territory nobody controls, and come back as pages that did not exist until you asked for them. Underfoot, the operating system quietly keeps the whole castle from falling over.
objectives: Describe what an operating system manages, and what a process is
Explain how DNS, IP, and TCP get a message across the internet
Read HTTP requests, responses, and status codes
Trace the request/response cycle from a click to a rendered page
Explain APIs, web frameworks and templates, and the cloud service models

sets.title: Cybersecurity — Defending Systems
sets.description: The CIA triad (confidentiality, integrity, availability), threat modeling, SQL injection and parameterized queries, XSS and input escaping/validation, hashing vs. encryption and password salting, and secret management (.gitignore, environment variables).

intro.story: Something has been getting into the archive. Not by force — by walking up to the gate and saying exactly the right words. In this wing you learn the attacks by running them yourself, because a defence you have never seen defeated is a defence you do not understand.
objectives: Apply the CIA triad to judge what a given breach actually broke
Explain and prevent SQL injection and cross-site scripting
Store passwords properly with hashing and salting, and say why encryption differs
Keep secrets out of code with environment variables and .gitignore
Explain HTTPS, certificates, input validation, and defence in depth

sets.title: AI, Machine Learning & Ethics
sets.description: Machine learning vs. traditional code, supervised vs. unsupervised learning, perceptron mechanics and neural networks, LLMs (tokens, training, next-token prediction, limitations), algorithmic bias and proxy variables, and AI accountability.

intro.story: The last chamber holds the Dragon itself — and it turns out to be neither a mind nor a monster, but a very large pile of arithmetic that learned its habits from whatever it was fed. Ada wants you to see exactly how it works before you decide how much to trust it.
objectives: Explain how machine learning differs from ordinary programming
Distinguish supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning
Compute a perceptron's output and say what its trained weights mean
Explain next-token prediction, and why LLMs hallucinate so fluently
Identify algorithmic bias, proxy variables, and the accountability gap

sets.title: Bonus: Python to Java 1 — Values, Types & the JVM
sets.description: Java for Python programmers, part 1: a whole Java program and what javac and the JVM each do; bytecode, write once run anywhere, the JIT compiler and garbage collection; declared types; integer division, casts and overflow; char, String and +; String methods and printf; and why teams choose Java or Python for different jobs.

intro.story: Past the last chamber the labyrinth keeps going, but the runes on the walls change: this wing is written in Java, the language of your next course. Ada reads both. She says nothing you learned in Python is wasted here. Java simply wants you to state things that Python let you leave unsaid, starting with the type of every value.
objectives: Read a whole Java program, and say what javac and the JVM each do
Explain what bytecode, the JIT compiler and the garbage collector each do, and when each one pays off
Declare variables with a type, and predict Java's arithmetic: integer division, casts and overflow
Build output with +, println and printf, and use Java's String methods
Give the real reasons a team would choose Java or Python for a job

sets.title: Bonus: Python to Java 2 — Decisions, Loops, Methods & Tests
sets.description: Part 2: if / else if with &&, || and !, braces instead of indentation, the three-part for loop in place of range, while and do-while, switch, methods with return types and void, overloading in place of default arguments, block scope, and comparing Strings with equals. Then a program of several classes, with main, static calls, args and Javadoc, and testing a method with JUnit.

intro.story: Nia has followed you into the Java wing, chalk in hand. The doors still open on conditions and the stairs still loop back, but every block is now fenced in braces, and every method has to say what it hands back. Nia wants you to find out which of your Python habits still work here, and which ones quietly give the wrong answer. Professor Flint will then show you how to check what you have written, with tests.
objectives: Write if / else if / else and switch, with Java's &&, || and !
Turn a Python for loop over range into Java's three-part for, and use while and do-while
Write methods with a return type or void, overload them, and explain block scope
Split a program into classes, start it from main, and call a static method through its class's name
Test a method with JUnit at its boundaries, and read what a failing test reports

sets.title: Bonus: Python to Java 3 — Collections, Classes & Packages
sets.description: Part 3: arrays and ArrayLists, Integer and not int, HashMap and HashSet in place of dict and set, and a list of dictionaries rebuilt as a class with a constructor, private fields, getters and toString. Then programs of many classes: one public class per file and one job per class, List as an interface, packages and imports, the four access levels, and the folders Maven and Gradle expect.

intro.story: Zoya's workshop has a Java bench now. The lists and dictionaries you built in Python are here too, under other names and with stricter rules: an array cannot grow, a list must say what it holds, and a dictionary of named values becomes a class. Zoya wants you to rebuild your Python data in Java, one piece at a time. Then Professor Flint will show you how a program of many classes is laid out in folders.
objectives: Use arrays, whose length is fixed, and ArrayLists, which grow, and explain why a list holds Integer rather than int
Translate a dict into a HashMap and a set into a HashSet, and handle a missing key
Rebuild a Python list of dictionaries as a Java class with private fields, a constructor, getters and toString
Split a program into classes with one job each, one public class per file, and declare variables by interface, such as List
Put classes in packages and folders, import them, choose an access level, and find your way around the standard Maven and Gradle layout

sets.title: Bonus: Python to Java 4 — The Big Ideas & Building a Project
sets.description: Part 4: recursion and the call stack; polymorphism, @Override, abstract classes and interfaces, and how an interface makes a class testable; exceptions with try, catch, finally and throw, checked and unchecked; build tools, dependencies and JARs; and sorting errors into those javac finds before a program runs and those found only while it runs.

intro.story: At the deepest level of the Java wing, four mentors are waiting. Nia will show you methods that call themselves. Zoya will show you one call that different objects answer in different ways, and Professor Flint will show you how that keeps a big program testable, and how one command turns its many files into a single program. Kaelen will show you what Java does when something goes wrong. Ada waits at the end with one question about all of it: did Java find the problem before the program ran, or only while it ran?
objectives: Trace a recursive Java method down to its base case and back up, and say what a StackOverflowError reports
Predict which version of a method runs when a variable's type and its object's class differ, and use @Override, abstract classes and interfaces
Use an interface to swap a predictable stand-in for a random part, so that a class can be tested
Catch, throw and declare exceptions, and tell a checked exception from an unchecked one
Explain what a build tool does with a build file, its dependencies, the tests and a JAR
Sort errors into those javac finds before a program runs, those found while it runs, and those never reported

description: SQL from the first SELECT to joins, design, transactions and security.

sets.title: Database Foundations
sets.description: Data vs. information, flat files vs. databases, data models, deployment choices, and first SQLite notebook queries.

sets.title: Introduction to SQL: SELECT
sets.description: SELECT and FROM, DISTINCT, WHERE, ORDER BY, NULL handling, LIKE patterns, aliases, aggregates, and SQLite syntax basics.

sets.title: Joins and Set Operations
sets.description: ERDs, keys, junction tables, INNER and LEFT JOIN, CROSS JOIN, and combining results with UNION, INTERSECT, and EXCEPT.

sets.title: Super Select: Advanced Retrieval
sets.description: Complex schemas, GROUP BY and HAVING, subqueries, CASE and PRINTF, JSON in SQLite, Big O intuition, and backup and recovery planning.

sets.title: Database Design
sets.description: Design levels, ERDs, keys, normalization, constraints, SQLite typing, and core DDL.

sets.title: Writing Data
sets.description: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, constraints, foreign-key delete actions, soft deletes, triggers, and access paths in SQLite.

sets.title: Views, CTEs & Governance
sets.description: SQLite views and CTEs, plus data classification, privacy, and governance basics.

sets.title: Performance & Transactions
sets.description: Indexes, query plans, B-trees, transaction control, locking, and monitoring basics in SQLite.

sets.title: PostgreSQL Basics
sets.description: PostgreSQL compared with SQLite: server use cases, stricter types, schema changes, roles, procedures, and analytics.

sets.title: Database Security
sets.description: CIA triad, database threats, encryption, access control, masking, auditing, retention, and layered defenses.

sets.title: Architecture, Deployment & Testing
sets.description: Database design patterns, deployment choices, operational trade-offs, and testing basics for schemas and systems.

sets.title: SQLite Final Project
sets.description: A capstone SQLite project from planning and ERDs through schema design, queries, testing, and documentation.

description: A first programming course in Java, from printing a line to classes, streams and GUIs.

sets.title: Java Review Mix
sets.description: 30 random questions drawn evenly from all Java sets. Each try gives a new mix.

sets.title: Hour of Java
sets.description: A gentle first tour of Java for people who have never programmed: printing, variables, a little arithmetic, one if, one loop, and a first method of your own. Short lessons, easy questions, and every kind of question in the game.

intro.story: Just inside the labyrinth gate the Recursive Dragon has left its smallest hoard: the first few ideas of Java, each one only half learned. Ada the Chief Artificer and Nia the Logic-Weaver are waiting at the workbench to walk you through them, and every kind of monster in the Guild's bestiary has turned up to test you once.
objectives: Describe what a program is, and how Java code becomes something a computer can run
Write statements that print text, and tell print from println
Create a variable of the right type and trace how its value changes line by line
Join text to a value with +, and do simple arithmetic
Predict which block of an if or an if-else runs
Count how many times a simple loop repeats
Write the inside of a small method and return its answer

sets.title: Java Basics
sets.description: Write, compile and run a first Java program; print text with print, println and escape sequences; store values in variables of the five basic types; do arithmetic; and fix the mistakes the compiler catches.

intro.story: The Guild's Java forge is lit, and Ada hands you a blank scroll: before anything grand, you must make the machine store a value and do honest arithmetic with it. The dragon's hoard is full of half-learned sums — a 7 / 2 that somebody swore was 3.5, a receipt that added 2 and 3 and got 23 — and Nia will have you trace each line until none of them can fool you.
objectives: Compile and run a Java program with javac and java, and say what each step produces
Name the parts of a program: the class line, the main method, statements and braces
Print text with print and println, using the escape sequences \n, \t and \"
Declare and initialize variables, choosing between int, double, String, char and boolean
Evaluate arithmetic that uses + - * / and %, with the usual order of operations
Join text to a value with +, and get the spaces right
Read a compiler error, find the line it names, and fix a missing semicolon, quote, brace or declaration
Write one-line method bodies that return the result of arithmetic or joined text

sets.title: Control Flow
sets.description: Conditions that are true or false, if / else if / else, the comparison operators, && and ||, arrays and their indexes, and for and while loops.

intro.story: Past the first hall the labyrinth stops running in a straight line: doors that open only on a condition, corridors that loop back on themselves, and rows of numbered chests the Dragon has stuffed with half-counted treasure. Nia the Logic-Weaver waits at the first fork with a stick of chalk, ready to show you how to trace every path instead of guessing at it.
objectives: Predict which block of an if, an if-else or an else-if chain runs
Write conditions with the six comparison operators, and tell = from ==
Combine conditions with && and ||, using parentheses when they are mixed
Create an array, reach its elements by index from 0, and find the last one with length - 1
Count the passes of a for loop, and use one to visit every element of an array
Trace a while loop, and recognise one that never ends
Write short methods that choose and loop, returning an answer on every path

sets.title: Algorithms
sets.description: What makes a list of steps an algorithm, flowcharts, linear search, the accumulator patterns, break, continue and switch, best and worst cases, and binary search.

intro.story: Past the loop-forges lies the Hall of Patterns, where the dragon hoards half-learned recipes: sums that start in the wrong place, searches that trust unsorted shelves, swaps that lose a value on the way. Nia the Logic-Weaver will not let you memorise them. She makes you move the markers and trace every pass by hand, until the patterns are yours.
objectives: Say what an algorithm is, and recognise instructions too vague to be one
Read a flowchart and trace what it does
Trace linear search, including the boolean flag and the -1 that means “not found”
Trace sum, count, product, minimum, maximum and text-building accumulators, and spot a wrong starting value
Predict the effect of break and continue in a loop
Trace a switch statement, including a missing break
Give the best and worst case of linear search, and explain why binary search needs so few probes
Write search, counting and accumulator loops as methods that return their answer

sets.title: Methods, Strings & Recursion
sets.description: Defining and calling methods, parameters and return values, void, scope and why a parameter is a copy, overloading, the built-in String methods, and a first look at recursion.

intro.story: Deeper in the Guild's workshops the artificers stop building one enormous machine and start building small named ones that call each other. Nia the Logic-Weaver keeps a ledger of exactly what passes between them, because the dragon's hoard is full of half-learned ideas about what a method can reach out and change. Learn what really crosses the counter, and then meet the strangest machine of all: one that calls itself.
objectives: Read a method line, and say what each part of it promises
Call a method with arguments, and trace what comes back
Tell a void method from one that returns a value, and predict the effect of return
Explain why a variable declared in one method cannot be seen in another, and why changing a parameter does not change the caller's variable
Recognise overloaded methods and say which one a call runs
Use String methods, chain them, and remember that they return a new String
Trace a recursive method down to its base case and back
Write methods that take values in and return an answer

sets.title: Casts, Null & Imports
sets.description: Imports, casting and rounding, integer overflow, wrapper classes, null and NullPointerException, empty and blank Strings, validating input, the enhanced for loop, and 2D arrays.

intro.story: The dragon's hoard here is made of things that are almost the same: a 4 that should have been 4.5, a letter that is secretly a number, an empty scroll and no scroll at all. Nia and Ada have laid the near-twins side by side on the workbench, because the Guild's rule is that you may not use a conversion until you can say what it throws away.
objectives: Say which names need an import, and what an import does
Predict the result of a cast, and choose between a cast, Math.round, Math.floor and Math.ceil
Recognise integer overflow, and do the arithmetic in long to avoid it
Explain autoboxing and unboxing, and use the wrapper classes to parse text into numbers
Tell null from an empty or a blank String, and check for them in an order that cannot crash
Read a loop that validates input with hasNextInt, and say why it discards bad input
Use an enhanced for loop, and say when a loop with an index is needed instead
Index, measure and loop over a 2D array
Write methods that are handed null, or that return it

sets.title: Collections: Lists, Sets and Maps
sets.description: Java's collections: ArrayList and its methods, looping over a collection, arrays against ArrayLists, LinkedList, HashSet, HashMap, the Collections class, and choosing the right collection for a job.

intro.story: The Dragon's hoard is not gold but clutter: heaps of half-sorted names, duplicate trinkets, and ledgers with every entry written twice. Zoya the Golem-Shaper waits among the shelves with three kinds of container, and they insist you learn what each one does to the things you put in it before you trust it with anything you want back.
objectives: Declare lists, sets and maps with generics, and say which family each collection belongs to
Predict the contents and size of a list after add, set, get and both forms of remove
Loop over a collection, and say which changes break a for-each loop
Choose between an array and an ArrayList, and convert one to the other
Use the two ends of a LinkedList as a queue
Explain how a Set treats duplicates and how a Map treats a repeated key, and count things with a map
Check what get returns before using it, and tell containsKey from containsValue
Use Collections.sort, reverse, max, min and frequency, and say what binarySearch requires
Write methods that take and return lists, sets and maps

sets.title: Objects and Classes
sets.description: Classes and objects: fields and methods, constructors and this, private fields with getters and setters, objects that work together, lists of objects, and toString.

intro.story: Zoya the Golem-Shaper's workshop is lined with clay figures, each stamped from the same mould and each holding its own spark. The dragon hoards half-learned ideas about objects: that two names must mean two things, that == looks inside, that private means frozen. Shape your own classes here, and leave the workshop knowing exactly which object every variable is tied to.
objectives: Tell a class from an object, and an object's state from its behavior
Make objects with new, and use their fields and methods with a dot
Write constructors, including more than one, and use this to tell a field from a parameter
Explain what private protects, and write getters and setters that guard a field
Hand one object to another, and have it use the other's public methods
Keep objects in an ArrayList, and loop over them
Write toString, and say where Java calls it for you
Write a method of a class, and then a whole class, to pass tests that use its objects

sets.title: Inheritance and Polymorphism
sets.description: Inheritance: extends and super(…), what a subclass inherits, overriding and super.method(), the class Object with toString and equals, polymorphism, instanceof and casts, abstract classes, and interfaces.

intro.story: In the Golem-Shaper's foundry every new golem begins from an older mould, and Zoya will not let you cast one until you can say exactly what it inherits and what it changes. The dragon's hoard here is a heap of half-learned family trees: constructors that ran in an order nobody predicted, and casts that promised more than the object could deliver. Learn to read the tag on the variable and the creature wearing it, and the heap sorts itself.
objectives: Write a subclass with extends, and say what it inherits and what it does not
Call a superclass constructor with super(…), and trace the order constructors run in
Override a method, tell overriding from overloading, and build on the superclass's version with super.method()
Override toString and equals, and say what the inherited ones do
Predict which version of a method runs when a superclass variable holds a subclass object
Check an object's type with instanceof before casting down
Write and extend an abstract class, and implement interfaces
Write a subclass, an override, and a class that implements an interface, to pass tests

sets.title: Exceptions
sets.description: How a Java program comes to run: javac, bytecode, the JVM, the stack and the heap, static and instance. Then what happens when a running program goes wrong: exceptions, try/catch/finally, the order of catch blocks, checked vs. unchecked, propagation, throw and throws, and exception classes of your own.

intro.story: Deep in the dungeon the machines stop failing quietly: they fling their failures at you as exceptions, and the dragon has hoarded every half-learned way of ignoring them. Nia the Logic-Weaver starts further back, with how a program comes to run at all, and then will not let you swallow a single exception. Trace where each one is thrown, which lines it abandons on the way up, and who (if anyone) is ready to catch it.
objectives: Put in order the steps from source code to a running program: javac, bytecode, class loading, the JVM
Say what lives on the stack, on the heap and in the method area, and where static and instance members belong
Tell the mistakes the compiler catches from the ones that wait until the program runs
Trace the flow of try, catch and finally, including when nothing is thrown and when nothing matches
Order catch blocks from specific to general, and read an exception's message with getMessage()
Distinguish checked from unchecked exceptions, and use throw and throws correctly
Follow an exception up the call stack, and decide where it is best caught
Write a try/catch, a finally, a method that throws, and an exception class of your own, to pass tests

sets.title: Lambdas & Streams
sets.description: Lambdas, an interface with one method, Predicate, Function and Consumer; then stream pipelines: filter, map, collect, count, findFirst and Optional, the matchers, sorted, limit and skip, mapToInt with sum, max, min and average, and the mistakes that catch everyone once.

intro.story: Deep in the labyrinth the Recursive Dragon hoards half-learned loops: the same for-loop copied a hundred times, each with its own counter and its own bug. Zoya the Golem-Shaper and Nia the Logic-Weaver have a better tool on their bench, a pipeline that says WHAT you want from a collection and leaves the looping to Java. Learn to read one station at a time and the hoard comes apart.
objectives: Say what makes a stream pipeline declarative, and match its parts to the loop it replaces
Write a lambda in its long and short forms, for a Predicate, a Function, a Consumer or an interface of your own
Trace a pipeline stage by stage, following both the elements and their type
Choose between filter and map, and end a pipeline with forEach, collect, count, findFirst or a matcher
Sort with sorted, keep or drop elements with limit and skip, and say why their order matters
Total, average and find the extremes of a stream with mapToInt, and open the Optional they come in
Predict when a lazy pipeline runs, and recognise a stream used twice and a null inside a lambda
Write a lambda, and a pipeline of up to five stages, to pass tests

sets.title: GUIs & Event-Driven Programming
sets.description: Swing windows as a first event-driven program: components and layout managers, listeners written as lambdas, the event-dispatch thread and why windows freeze, and MVC for keeping logic testable.

intro.story: Every program you have written so far ran from its first line to its last and stopped. In this wing the Dragon keeps machines that do the opposite: windows that sit and wait, and run a scrap of your code only when someone touches them. Zoya the Golem-Shaper and Ada are here to show you who calls that code, on which thread, and where the real logic should live.
objectives: Build a Swing window from a JFrame, components, pack() and setVisible(true), and say what breaks when a call is missing
Predict where BorderLayout, FlowLayout and GridLayout put components, and how they react to resizing
Write listeners as lambdas and trace when, and how many times, a handler runs
Explain the event-dispatch thread, SwingUtilities.invokeLater, and why a slow handler freezes the window
Split a GUI program into model, view and controller so that its logic can be tested without a window

sets.title: Git, Testing & Working with AI
sets.description: The working habits around the code: the everyday Git and GitHub cycle, branches and merge conflicts, JUnit tests that can actually fail, debugging from a stack trace, and using agentic AI assistants without trusting them blindly.

intro.story: The Dragon's last trick is not a puzzle but a mess: half-saved work, code nobody checked, and confident voices echoing answers that were never tested. Professor Flint keeps the Guild's ledgers and proving-grounds, where every change is recorded and every claim is tried; Elder Omu, the Oracle of Echoes, will teach you when an echo can be believed. Leave this wing working the way artificers do when other people depend on what they build.
objectives: Move a change through Git's working tree, staging area, local history and remote, and predict what git status will show
Work on a branch, resolve a merge conflict by hand, and propose the result in a pull request
Write JUnit 5 tests with arrange-act-assert, in the right argument order, that cover edge cases and are able to fail
Read a stack trace down to the line in your own code, and choose between stepping, printing and bisecting
Verify what an AI assistant tells you by running and testing it, and decide what to delegate and what to keep

description: Preparation for the CompTIA Network+ (N10-010) exam: twelve sets that cover every objective, each taught by the Guild's mentors.

sets.title: Network+ Review Mix
sets.description: 30 random questions drawn evenly from all twelve Network+ sets. Each try gives a new mix.

sets.title: Appliances, Protocols & Models
sets.description: The ground floor of networking: the OSI seven-layer and TCP/IP four-layer models, PDUs, encapsulation and decapsulation; routers, switches, access points, wireless controllers, load balancers and servers; traditional and next-generation firewalls, IDS and IPS, proxies, VPN and NAC; TCP and UDP with well-known and dynamic ports; DNS, DHCP, NTP, SSH, RDP, SMB, SIP, HTTP, ARP and ICMP; IPsec (IKE, AH, ESP) and GRE; and unicast, multicast, anycast and broadcast.

intro.story: The Guild's message-roads begin here, at the mouth of the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth, where every courier learns the layers a message is wrapped in and the boxes that pass it along. Tariq the Beacon-Courier walks you through the models, the appliances and the protocols, and Val the Ward-Smith shows you the guards, sensors and tunnels that decide which traffic may pass.
objectives: Map the OSI and TCP/IP models, name each layer's PDU, and trace encapsulation and decapsulation
Tell routers, switches, access points, wireless controllers, load balancers and servers apart by the job each does
Compare traditional and next-generation firewalls, IDS and IPS, forward and reverse proxies, VPN and NAC
Contrast TCP with UDP, and read well-known, registered and dynamic ports in a socket pair
Give the job, transport and port of DNS, DHCP, NTP, SSH, RDP, SMB, SIP and HTTP, and what ARP and ICMP do
Explain IPsec's IKE, AH and ESP, GRE, and the four traffic types: unicast, multicast, anycast and broadcast

sets.title: Media, Transceivers & IP Addressing
sets.description: The physical link and the address on it: UTP, STP and plenum copper, single-mode and multimode fiber, wireless media and media converters; LC, SC, ST, RJ45 and RJ11 connectors; SFP and QSFP transceivers; installation considerations from attenuation to budget; classful and classless IPv4, CIDR, subnetting and VLSM plans; RFC 1918, loopback and APIPA; and IPv6 against address exhaustion, with SLAAC, dual stack, tunneling and NAT64.

intro.story: Below the Guild's first halls, the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth is wired with every kind of cable and numbered with every kind of address, and half of it is wrong. Ada the Chief Artificer knows the wires and the optics, Nia the Logic-Weaver turns masks into arithmetic, and Tariq the Beacon-Courier carries packets across the border between IPv4 and IPv6.
objectives: Choose copper, fiber or wireless media from distance, noise, climate, bandwidth and budget
Identify LC, SC, ST, RJ45 and RJ11 connectors, and match SFP and QSFP optics
Convert masks to prefixes, and count hosts, subnets and block sizes
Find any host's network, broadcast and usable range, and build a VLSM plan
Recognize RFC 1918, loopback and APIPA addresses and what each reveals
Explain how IPv6, SLAAC, dual stack, tunneling and NAT64 answer address exhaustion

sets.title: Cloud, Topologies & Modern Networks
sets.description: Star, hub-and-spoke, mesh, two- and three-tier and spine-and-leaf designs; north-south and east-west traffic; intranet, extranet, DMZ, IoT, OT/SCADA, air-gapped networks and wireless bridges; hypervisors, containers, microservices and NFV; cloud deployment and service models, elasticity, VPN, non-transitive peering and interconnects; VXLAN and DCI; SDN and SD-WAN; CDNs; REST, SOAP and GraphQL, IaC and Git; and Zero Trust.

intro.story: Past the wiring closets, the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth stops being made of cable and starts being made of software: fabrics drawn on top of fabrics, clouds rented by the hour, whole networks rebuilt from a file. Tariq the Beacon-Courier maps the shapes and overlays, Professor Flint turns configs into code, and Val the Ward-Smith makes every request prove itself.
objectives: Choose a topology and architecture, and tell north-south from east-west traffic
Place IoT, OT/SCADA, DMZ, extranet and air-gapped networks correctly
Compare hypervisors, containers, microservices and NFV
Match cloud models to a need, and connect by VPN, peering or interconnect
Explain VXLAN, SDN and SD-WAN policy, and how a CDN offloads an origin
Automate with APIs, IaC and Git, and apply Zero Trust to every request

sets.title: Routing & Switching
sets.description: Routing tables and static, default and dynamic routes; route announcement; route selection by prefix length, administrative distance and metric; OSPF, EIGRP and BGP; NAT, PAT and FHRP; VLANs (default, native, management), access and trunk ports, 802.1Q tags, sub-interfaces and SVIs; MAC tables and STP root election, port roles, states and modes; LACP and MLAG; port mirroring; duplex; err-disable; PoE; CDP and LLDP.

intro.story: Past the Guild's lower halls, the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth becomes a maze of junctions where every corridor is a route and every door a switch port. Tariq the Beacon-Courier knows which way each packet should go, and Nia the Logic-Weaver can prove why one path beats another and which switch rules the tree.
objectives: Read a routing table and tell connected, static, default and dynamic routes apart
Pick the route a router uses by prefix length, administrative distance and metric
Compare OSPF, EIGRP and BGP, and explain NAT, PAT and FHRP
Configure VLANs, access and trunk ports, native VLANs and inter-VLAN routing
Predict the STP root bridge, port roles and port states
Apply link aggregation, port mirroring, duplex, err-disable, PoE and CDP/LLDP settings

sets.title: Wireless & Physical Installations
sets.description: Wi-Fi 5, 6, 6E and 7 in the 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz bands, channels and band steering; BSS/ESS, autonomous vs lightweight APs, controllers, LPI and standard-power APs, extenders and antennas; point-to-point, point-to-multipoint and mesh; cellular and satellite; WPA2/WPA3, AES vs TKIP, guest networks and captive portals; MDF, IDF, demarc, patch and fiber panels, colocation and MMR; power, UPS and generators; cooling; fire suppression; physical security; safety.

intro.story: Past the routing halls, the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth opens onto the Guild's outer works: towers that must speak to each other through the air, and the rooms where every cable comes home. Tariq the Beacon-Courier tunes the radios here, and Ada the Chief Artificer keeps the power, the cooling and the doors.
objectives: Choose Wi-Fi generations, bands and non-overlapping channels for a site
Build Wi-Fi from BSSs and ESSs, with the right APs, controllers and antennas
Secure Wi-Fi with WPA2/WPA3 and AES, and run guest networks behind captive portals
Pick point-to-point, point-to-multipoint, mesh, cellular or satellite links
Name the telecom spaces and panels from the demarc to the desk
Size power, UPS and generator backup, and control heat, humidity and airflow
Apply fire suppression, physical security and safety practices

sets.title: Policies, Documentation & Monitoring
sets.description: How a network is run and watched: SOPs, the knowledge base, physical and logical diagrams, heat maps and the BC/DR plan; SLAs, MSAs, NDAs, licensing, warranty, lock-in and lock-out; change management, service windows, ticketing, backups and incident response; AUP, BYOD and password policies, compliance, KRIs, asset inventory and the life cycle to EOS; SNMPv2c/v3, syslog, SIEM, packet capture, flow analysis, synthetic tests, baselines and IPAM.

intro.story: Deep in the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth the Guild keeps an archive where every cable, contract and change is written down, and a watchtower where every device reports in. Master Kaelen guards the records that let anyone fix a network its builder has left, and Tariq the Beacon-Courier reads the signals that warn of trouble before the users do.
objectives: Choose the right document: SOP, knowledge base, physical or logical diagram, heat map, or BC/DR plan
Read SLAs, MSAs and NDAs, do SLA downtime arithmetic, and manage licensing, warranties, lock-in and lock-out
Run a change through change management and a service window, with tickets, tested backups and incident response
Apply AUP, BYOD and password policies, internal and external compliance, and KRIs
Keep the asset inventory and manage the life cycle: patches, OS and firmware updates, EOL, EOS and decommissioning
Monitor with SNMPv2c/v3, syslog, log aggregators and SIEM, and compute utilization from counters
Pick packet capture, flow analysis, synthetic tests, baselines, performance tools, IPAM or discovery for each question

sets.title: Continuity, Remote Access & AI
sets.description: Staying up, getting in and using AI safely: active-active and active-passive HA, fault tolerance, stress testing; MTBF, MTTR, RTO, RPO; cold, warm, hot and mobile sites; backups and restores; tabletop, bubble, parallel and validation tests, vendor SLAs; site-to-site and client-to-site VPNs, split and full tunneling; in-band and out-of-band management, console, crash cart, SSH, RDP, HTTPS, jump boxes, APIs; AI types, uses, policy and security.

intro.story: Deep in the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth the Guild keeps its fallback halls: the standby that wakes when the active one falls, the vault of backups, the hidden passage for when every main road is blocked. Val the Ward-Smith keeps the recovery plans, Tariq the Beacon-Courier the roads and back doors, and Elder Omu the new oracles, whose answers must be checked before anyone acts on them.
objectives: Compare active-active, active-passive and fault-tolerant designs, and compute MTBF, MTTR and availability
Set RTO and RPO, choose a cold, warm, hot or mobile site, and plan backups and restores
Tell tabletop, bubble, parallel and validation tests apart, and check a vendor's SLA
Choose site-to-site or client-to-site VPNs, with split or full tunneling
Reach devices in-band and out-of-band: console, crash cart, SSH, RDP, HTTPS, jump boxes and API calls
Classify AI types and uses, and apply an AUP, results verification and AI security controls

sets.title: Security Concepts & Compliance
sets.description: The vocabulary and the paperwork of network security: risk, threat, vulnerability, zero-days and CVEs, attack surface and vector, the CIA triad; encryption in transit, at rest and in use; PKI and self-signed certificates; AAA, MFA, SSO with SAML, PAM, geofencing; RADIUS vs TACACS+; secure replacements for cleartext protocols; hardening, baselines, HIDS and HIPS; data locality, BYOD, regulations, audits, frameworks and the four risk strategies.

intro.story: Past the labyrinth's wiring closets lies a hall of locks, ledgers and seals, where the Recursive Dragon's agents probe for the password sent in cleartext and the certificate nobody trusts. Val the Ward-Smith teaches the words, the keys and the rules the Guild lives by, and Tariq the Beacon-Courier shows what each protocol looks like on the wire.
objectives: Tell risk, threat, vulnerability, exploit, attack surface and attack vector apart, and name zero-days and CVEs
Match encryption to data in transit, at rest and in use, and trace a certificate chain to a trusted root
Replace cleartext protocols with their secure versions and ports
Apply AAA, MFA, SSO with SAML, PAM and geofencing, and choose between RADIUS and TACACS+
Harden devices to a security baseline and tell HIDS from HIPS
Weigh data locality, BYOD, regulations, audits and frameworks, and pick a risk strategy

sets.title: Attacks & Defenses
sets.description: Network attacks and their impacts: social engineering, DoS/DDoS, spoofing, VLAN hopping, ARP and DHCP poisoning, exploits, overflows, ping sweeping, rubber-duck USB, password sniffing, evil twins, malicious code, vandalism, and hijacking; and the defenses - RBAC, least privilege, ACLs, patch management, honeypots/honeynets, vulnerability scanning, segmentation, hardening, port security, DHCP snooping, ARP inspection, 802.1X, and key management.

intro.story: Deep in the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth the Guild keeps a hall of broken wards, each a lesson in how a network falls. Val the Ward-Smith names the attacks and their cost, from a whispered phishing lure to a botnet's flood, while Tariq the Beacon-Courier shows how a switch, rightly set, turns every Layer 2 trick back on itself.
objectives: Identify social-engineering, network, switch, and wireless attacks from their symptoms
Weigh the technical and business impacts of a breach, from exfiltration to lost continuity
Harden switches with port security, DHCP snooping, ARP inspection, and 802.1X
Apply RBAC, least privilege, segmentation, and ordered ACLs
Use patch management, vulnerability scanning, honeypots, and sound key management

sets.title: Troubleshooting Cabling, Interfaces & Wireless
sets.description: Interface counters (CRC, runts, giants, overruns, drops); copper length, attenuation and crosstalk; fiber faults, transceivers and DOM light levels; interface states and err-disabled, admin-down and suspended ports; duplex, speed and MTU/jumbo mismatches; PoE standards and power budgets; Wi-Fi signal, SNR, noise, co-channel and rogue interference, spectrum, roaming, AP placement, antennas and TX/RX levels.

intro.story: Deep in the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth, the Guild's links are up but sick: ports counting errors, runs too long, optics starved of light, and access points shouting past clients that cannot answer. Ada the Chief Artificer reads the copper, glass and power; Tariq the Beacon-Courier reads the ports and the air.
objectives: Diagnose a wired link from its interface counters
Find copper, fiber and transceiver faults, from crosstalk to dirty connectors
Read interface states and recover err-disabled, shut and suspended ports
Spot duplex, speed and MTU mismatches, and test a jumbo-frame path
Choose PoE standards and keep a switch within its power budget
Troubleshoot Wi-Fi signal, interference, roaming, placement and antennas

sets.title: Troubleshooting Devices & Services
sets.description: Troubleshooting the services and devices a network runs on: APIPA, masks and gateways; DHCP exhaustion, missing options, relays and lease expiry; DNS zones, records, recursion, authoritative answers, secondaries and the hosts file; NTP drift and NAT exhaustion; broadcast storms, VLANs, one-way links, STP and virtual switches; routing loops, black holes and asymmetry; firewall rule order and NAC; voice, QoS and device management.

intro.story: Deeper in the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth every lantern still burns, yet nothing reaches anywhere: addresses come from nowhere, names point at the wrong doors, and packets walk in circles. Tariq the Beacon-Courier walks you through the services and devices that fail this way, and Val the Ward-Smith shows you firewalls and NAC doing exactly what they were told.
objectives: Diagnose addressing and DHCP faults from ipconfig output and server logs
Trace DNS failures through the hosts file, resolvers, zones and records
Recognize switching, virtualization and routing faults from tables and traces
Find firewall rule-order, classification and NAC policy mistakes
Tell latency, jitter, loss and capacity apart, and fix voice with VLANs and QoS
Keep devices reachable, consistently versioned, baselined and on time

sets.title: Troubleshooting Tools & Commands
sets.description: The hands-on diagnostic toolkit: CLI commands (ping, traceroute/tracert, netstat, nmap, netcat, nslookup, dig, tcpdump, ipconfig/ip, arp), packet capture and packet/protocol analyzers, NetFlow, network taps versus SPAN ports, hardware tools (toner and probe, spectrum analyzer, log collector), and reading real display outputs - route tables, ARP caches, netstat, traceroute hops, and nmap scans.

intro.story: At the labyrinth's workbench the Recursive Dragon leaves only symptoms, never answers. Tariq, Ada, and Nia hand each apprentice the toolkit the Guild lives by: a command to ask the question, a device to find the fault in the wire or the air, and the patience to read every column the tools print back.
objectives: Choose the right CLI tool - ping, traceroute, netstat, nmap, netcat, nslookup, dig, tcpdump, ipconfig/ip, arp - and type it correctly on Windows or Linux
Capture packets and read them in a protocol analyzer, and know when NetFlow's flow summary is enough
Pick hardware tools: a toner and probe for copper, a spectrum analyzer for RF, a tap or SPAN for a monitoring feed, a log collector for events
Read display outputs - route tables, ARP caches, netstat, traceroute hops, nmap scans - to find the fault
Match a symptom to the one tool that diagnoses it fastest

description: Preparation for the CompTIA SecurityX (CAS-005) exam: twelve sets, one for each chapter of the open textbook Threats Real and Imagined, each taught by the Guild's mentors.

sets.title: SecurityX Review Mix
sets.description: 30 random questions drawn evenly from all twelve SecurityX sets. Each try gives a new mix.

sets.title: Security Governance, Compliance & Ethics
sets.description: Policies, standards, procedures and guidelines; RACI, separation of duties and management commitment; phishing, OPSEC and awareness programs that work; COBIT vs. ITIL; ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF 2.0, SOC 2, CIS and CSA CCM; assessments, audits and certifications; the data life cycle, legal holds, and masked or synthetic data for staging; GDPR, data sovereignty, CCPA, HIPAA, PCI DSS and the rest of the compliance landscape.

intro.story: Before the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth is a battle, it is a charter: who decided, who answers, and what was written down before anything went wrong. Val the Ward-Smith waits in the Guild's council hall with the rulebooks, and Master Kaelen keeps the archive where every record must be born, guarded and, in time, destroyed.
objectives: Place each requirement in the right tier: policy, standard, procedure or guideline
Assign RACI roles and spot failures of accountability, separation of duties and management commitment
Design an awareness program against phishing, social engineering and OPSEC leaks
Choose between COBIT, ITIL, ISO/IEC 27001, NIST CSF, SOC 2, CIS and CSA CCM for a stated need
Govern data across its life cycle and keep production data out of staging
Apply GDPR, data sovereignty, HIPAA, PCI DSS and the other regimes to a business scenario

sets.title: Risk Management & Threat Modeling
sets.description: The risk workflow, qualitative vs. quantitative analysis, SLE/ARO/ALE and a control's value, extreme-but-plausible scenarios, appetite vs. tolerance, treatment and silent acceptance, GRC tools; threat actors, vendor and subprocessor risk (Target HVAC); Kill Chain, Diamond, ATT&CK, STRIDE, CAPEC, OWASP, abuse cases, attack trees; attack surface, enumeration, legal holds, due diligence/care, M&A; breach response, BIA, RTO/RPO, backups, integrity and privacy.

intro.story: The Recursive Dragon's labyrinth has more doors than the Guild has guards, and no purse is deep enough to bar them all. Val the Ward-Smith will teach you to weigh each door, know who is likely to try it, and plan for the night one gives way; Nia the Logic-Weaver will check your sums and trace every path an attacker could take.
objectives: Calculate SLE, ARO and ALE, and use them to judge whether a control is worth its cost
Distinguish risk appetite from tolerance, and choose and document a risk treatment
Profile threat actors by motivation, resources and capabilities, and manage vendor and subprocessor risk
Apply the Kill Chain, Diamond Model, MITRE ATT&CK, STRIDE and attack trees to real scenarios
Map an attack surface through data flows, trust boundaries and enumeration, including legal and organizational change
Plan breach response and BCDR: set RTO and RPO, choose backups that survive ransomware, and verify integrity

sets.title: AI Threats & Governance
sets.description: Legal, privacy and ethical issues in AI adoption; explainable vs. non-explainable models; NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, MITRE ATLAS and the EU AI Act; deepfakes and the 2019 UK CEO voice fraud, AI-built exploits, polymorphic malware and phishing at scale; the OWASP LLM Top 10: prompt injection, output handling, model DoS, poisoning, inversion, theft, supply chain; DLP, AUPs, overreliance, excessive agency, guardrails and AI disclosure.

intro.story: Deeper in the labyrinth the Recursive Dragon has learned to speak in borrowed voices, and its scribes will take orders from any scroll they read. Elder Omu waits to show you how such oracles are built and how they are turned, and Val has the wards that stop them acting on a stranger's word.
objectives: Weigh the legal, privacy and ethical risks of adopting AI, including explainability
Counter deepfakes and AI-scaled attacks with out-of-band verification and behaviour-based defences
Distinguish direct and indirect prompt injection, and layer defences around the model
Trace the AI/ML pipeline and its trust boundaries, and place controls against poisoning, inversion and theft
Map model threats to their OWASP Top 10 for LLM entries and the controls that answer them
Govern AI use with DLP, an acceptable use policy, AI disclosure and least-privilege agents

sets.title: Security Architecture & Zero Trust
sets.description: Placing firewalls, IPS/IDS, taps, collectors, scanners, NAC, VPN, proxies, WAF, API gateways and CDNs; load balancing, active-active vs active-passive, scaling, persistence, availability and recovery order; Zero Trust PDP/PEP, continuous authorization, least privilege and attestation; microsegmentation, ZTNA, SASE, SD-WAN and SDN; boundaries, attack surface and sensor placement; classification, tagging, DLP and control-effectiveness metrics.

intro.story: Deep in the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth the Guild keeps a fortress whose walls were drawn long ago, and the dragon has learned to walk around them. Tariq will show you where each ward should really stand and how to build halls that fail without falling, and Val will teach you to trust no one for where they stand, only for what they can prove.
objectives: Place firewalls, IPS/IDS, taps, proxies, WAFs, API gateways, NAC and CDNs on the right trust boundary
Choose between active-active and active-passive designs, and size them for the loss of a node
Calculate the availability of components in series, and find hidden single points of failure
Explain PDPs, PEPs and implicit trust zones, and apply continuous authorization and attestation
Design segmentation, microsegmentation, ZTNA and SASE in place of a single perimeter
Place sensors and logging so that a crossed boundary is seen and a hunt can be tested
Drive DLP at rest, in transit and through discovery from classification tags, and measure risk movement

sets.title: Identity & Access Management
sets.description: Identity lifecycle (credential issuance, self-provisioning, joiner-mover-leaver, SCIM); federation, IdP/SP and SSO with SAML, OAuth 2.0 and OIDC; RBAC, rule-based, ABAC, MAC, DAC, PDP/PEP and conditional access; MFA, passkeys, biometrics, attestation and proofing; PAM, JIT, tiering, secrets rotation and trust policies; Golden SAML and identity TTPs; troubleshooting SAML, OIDC, Kerberos, 802.1X/EAP and SAE.

intro.story: Deeper in the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth the gates stop asking where you came from and ask only who you are, and the dragon has learned to forge the answer. Val keeps the Guild's ledger of identities and the keys that sign for them; Tariq carries the tokens and tickets that pass between the gates, and knows every way they go astray.
objectives: Design joiner, mover and leaver workflows driven by an authoritative source, with SCIM beside SSO
Choose among RBAC, rule-based, ABAC, MAC and DAC, and place PDPs, PEPs and conditional access
Trace SAML, OAuth 2.0 and OIDC flows, and read the claims in an assertion or ID token
Grade authentication evidence: MFA factors, passkeys, biometric error rates, attestation and NIST assurance levels
Apply PAM, just-in-time elevation, tiered administration, break-glass accounts and secrets rotation and deletion
Recognise identity attack paths, from credential dumping to Golden SAML, and the signals that expose them
Troubleshoot SAML, OIDC, Kerberos, 802.1X/EAP and SAE failures from the evidence

sets.title: Secure Systems Lifecycle & Hardware Assurance
sets.description: Functional vs. non-functional security requirements and the usability trade-off; linting and branch protection; CI/CD gates and tests (unit, integration, regression, retest, canary); SAST, DAST, IAST, RASP, formal methods; SCA, SBOMs, Log4Shell; supply chain and EOL; FIPS 140-3, Common Criteria; TPM, HSM, vTPM, enclaves, SEDs; Secure vs. Measured Boot and attestation; firmware, USB, memory and EM attacks; tamper detection, self-healing.

intro.story: The Recursive Dragon rarely breaks a gate; it slips through the ones that were built before anyone thought to guard them. In this wing Professor Flint shows how security is written into software from its first requirement to its release, and Ada the Chief Artificer goes beneath the operating system, to the chips and firmware where trust begins.
objectives: Write non-functional security requirements with testable acceptance criteria
Place linting, branch protection, SCA, SBOM generation, SAST, DAST, IAST and RASP in a CI/CD pipeline
Manage software and hardware supply chain risk and end-of-life with SBOMs, pinning, signing and provenance
Choose among TPM, HSM, vTPM, secure enclaves, SEDs and host-based encryption for a requirement
Distinguish Secure Boot from Measured Boot and read a PCR attestation result
Match firmware, USB, memory and electromagnetic attacks to the countermeasures that stop them

sets.title: Enterprise Cloud & Hybrid Security
sets.description: Shared responsibility across IaaS, PaaS and SaaS; cloud vs customer-managed keys (BYOK, HYOK, crypto-shredding) and BYOL; container, Kubernetes and serverless security; OIDC-federated CI/CD, Terraform, Ansible and policy-as-code; CASB modes and shadow IT; API gateways, rate limits, denial of wallet; Capital One SSRF and IMDSv2; data exposure, leakage, remanence; control families; hybrid links; FedRAMP.

intro.story: Deep in the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth, the Guild's vaults no longer stand behind its own walls: they are rented, shared, and reached by roads it does not own. Tariq knows exactly where the landlord's duty ends and yours begins, and Professor Flint guards the pipelines that build it all; both are waiting to show you where the dragon slips through.
objectives: Apply the shared responsibility model across IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
Choose among cloud-managed, customer-managed, BYOK and HYOK keys, and weigh BYOL
Secure container images, Kubernetes clusters and serverless functions with least privilege
Harden cloud delivery with OIDC-federated pipelines, Terraform, Ansible and policy-as-code
Govern cloud access and APIs with CASBs, gateways and rate limits, and trace the Capital One SSRF chain
Classify data exposure, leakage and remanence, and match proactive, preventative and detective controls to them
Plan hybrid connectivity and cloud service adoption, including FedRAMP

sets.title: Cryptography & PKI
sets.description: PKI architecture (offline roots, issuing CAs, RAs and CSRs), certificate extensions and templates, CRLs, OCSP stapling, ACME and Certificate Transparency; protecting data at rest, in transit and in use; sanitization, tokenization and anonymization; signatures, S/MIME, code signing and provenance; FIDO2 and key management; envelope encryption, AEAD, key stretching and splitting, forward secrecy, HE and SMPC; post-quantum cryptography.

intro.story: Every seal in the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth, every signed scroll and locked archive, traces back to a key someone has to guard. Val the Ward-Smith keeps the Guild's chains of trust, and she is waiting to show you how they are forged, how they break, and how to protect what they hold from an enemy patient enough to wait for tomorrow's machines.
objectives: Design a PKI hierarchy with an offline root, issuing CAs and RA vetting
Read a certificate's extensions and diagnose name, chain and revocation failures
Choose controls for data at rest, in transit, in use and at end of life
Apply tokenization, digital signatures, code signing and passwordless authentication
Explain envelope encryption, AEAD, key stretching, key splitting and forward secrecy
Plan a post-quantum migration around harvest-now-decrypt-later and hybrid key exchange

sets.title: Network, Endpoint & Infrastructure Engineering
sets.description: The operational layer where most breaches are won or lost: change and configuration management with a CMDB and the asset lifecycle; endpoint defense with EDR, HIPS/HIDS, host firewalls, EPM, application control, SELinux, and ASR; the TTPs behind credential dumping and evasion; troubleshooting IDS/IPS, routing, switching, VPN, and ACL faults; DNS, TLS, and email (SPF/DKIM/DMARC/S/MIME) security; DDoS mitigation; and MDM.

intro.story: Deeper in the Dragon's labyrinth the grand architecture gives way to plumbing: the endpoints people actually work on, the wires between them, and the inventory that is supposed to say what exists. Val the Ward-Smith and Tariq the Beacon-Courier wait here, because this is where clever designs meet the firewall rule in the wrong order and the agent switched off six months ago.
objectives: Run change and configuration management with a CMDB, a baseline, and the asset lifecycle
Choose endpoint controls - EDR, host firewall, EPM, allowlisting, SELinux, ASR - and read the TTPs they counter
Troubleshoot IDS/IPS, routing, switching, VPN, and ACL faults, and place sensors to see east-west movement
Secure DNS against poisoning and open zone transfers, and diagnose TLS cipher and PKI errors
Implement SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and S/MIME, and reason about DMARC alignment
Mitigate volumetric, protocol, and application-layer DDoS, and manage mobile devices with MDM and containerization

sets.title: Specialized, OT & Legacy Systems
sets.description: How operational technology differs from IT: SCADA, DCS, PLCs, HMIs, historians and building systems; the Purdue model, the industrial DMZ, and IEC 62443 zones and conduits; safety-first priorities, passive monitoring and unauthenticated industrial protocols; SoC and embedded design; RF and wireless segmentation; NERC CIP, FDA 524B, CMMC and other sector rules, with the Oldsmar case; and compensating controls for systems that cannot be patched.

intro.story: Deep in the labyrinth the Guild keeps its oldest machines: pumps and presses that have run for decades and were never built to meet a stranger on the wire. The Recursive Dragon loves them for exactly that reason. Ada the Chief Artificer and Tariq the Beacon-Courier are waiting at the control-room door to show you how to guard what you cannot rebuild.
objectives: Name the parts of an ICS (SCADA, DCS, PLC, RTU, HMI, historian) and place them on the Purdue model
Explain why OT ranks safety and availability first, and what that rules out
Separate IT from OT with an industrial DMZ, jump hosts, and IEC 62443 zones and conduits
Specify secure-by-design requirements for SoC-based and embedded devices
Choose RF technologies and wireless controls: WPA3-Enterprise, per-SSID VLANs, NAC, WIDS and per-device PSKs
Match utilities, healthcare, defense and transportation systems to the rules that govern them
Design and track compensating controls for obsolete, unsupported and constrained systems

sets.title: Security Operations, Monitoring & Threat Hunting
sets.description: The SIEM pipeline (collection, normalization and enrichment, tiered storage and retention, correlation), Windows event correlation and log queries, alert prioritisation and noise reduction, diverse data sources, dashboards and MTTD/MTTR, UEBA baselines, hypothesis-based hunting, honeypots and honey tokens, OSINT, ISACs and source reliability, STIX/TAXII and TIPs, IoCs vs IoAs, and Sigma, YARA and Snort rules.

intro.story: Deep in the labyrinth the Recursive Dragon leaves almost no tracks, only the faint ones every system writes down without being asked. Master Kaelen keeps those records, and Val has spent years learning which of them matter; between them they will teach you to read the logs, notice what is not normal, and go hunting before any alarm rings.
objectives: Trace a log through the SIEM pipeline and diagnose which stage has failed
Correlate Windows events and query raw logs to tell an attack from noise
Prioritise alerts by context, and cut noise without creating false negatives
Calculate false-positive rates, MTTD and log storage, and report outcome metrics
Use UEBA baselines, hypothesis-based hunts and deception to find hidden intruders
Evaluate and share threat intelligence with STIX, TAXII, a TIP and the TLP
Read and write Sigma, YARA and Snort detection logic

sets.title: Vulnerability Management, Automation & Incident Response
sets.description: Vulnerability classes and their root-cause fixes (injection, XSS, CSRF, SSRF, deserialization, TOCTOU, memory, misconfiguration, secrets), SBoM, VEX, CVE, CVSS vectors, KEV, EPSS and SCAP; scripting, cron and event triggers, webhooks, IaC, SOAR playbooks and approval gates, AI and automated patching; the IR lifecycle, exercises and insider cases; malware analysis, order of volatility, imaging, chain of custody and artifact sources.

intro.story: Deep in the Recursive Dragon's labyrinth the walls are scored with old breaches, and nearly every one traces back to a flaw somebody knew about and never fixed. Val will show you how flaws are named, scored and closed, Professor Flint how to make the fixing and the first response run on their own, and then Val again how to answer, and what to keep, when something gets through anyway.
objectives: Identify common vulnerability classes in code and configuration, and choose the root-cause fix for each
Read a CVSS vector, and prioritize findings with KEV, EPSS, SBoM and VEX data
Explain how SCAP, credentialed scanning and automated patching measure and reduce exposure
Automate security work with scripts, triggers, webhooks, IaC and SOAR playbooks, with guardrails
Order the incident-response lifecycle, and choose containment, eradication and recovery actions
Collect evidence by order of volatility, keep chain of custody, and pick the artifact that answers a question

description: Computing basics for the CompTIA Tech+ exam: what a computer is, number systems, hardware and ports.

sets.title: Computers and How They Count
sets.description: What makes something a computer (input, processing, output, and storage), the devices all around us from servers to smart doorbells, and the number systems computers count in.

intro.story: The Recursive Dragon has hidden tiny computers in everything: doorbells, cars, even the Guild's refrigerator. Ada the Chief Artificer will show you the four jobs every computer does, and Tariq the Beacon-Courier knows which of them talk to the world. Then the Dragon starts speaking in 0s and 1s, and Ada teaches you to count like a computer.
objectives: Define a computer by its four jobs: input, processing, output, and storage
Identify those jobs in everyday devices, from phones to robot vacuums
Describe common computing devices and what each is for, from servers to e-readers
Recognize Internet of Things devices and explain what makes them computers
Convert numbers between binary, decimal, hexadecimal, and octal, and tell which system a number is written in

sets.title: How Big, How Fast, and What's Inside
sets.description: Units of storage, throughput, and processor speed, and the parts inside a computer: processors, memory, drives, discs, and network cards.

intro.story: The Recursive Dragon has stuffed the Guild's vaults to bursting and choked its aqueducts. Ada the Chief Artificer will teach you to measure how big and how fast, from bits to petabytes and megahertz to gigahertz. Then she'll open up a computer and show you what every part inside it does, and why some of them forget.
objectives: Compare storage, throughput, and processor-speed units, from bits to petabytes and MHz to GHz
Convert between units, and work out how much fits and how long a download takes
Explain what each internal part does, from the motherboard and firmware to the GPU and network card
Distinguish volatile memory from non-volatile storage, and compare drives, discs, and flash
Choose storage for a job, and work out how many discs or drives a backup needs

sets.title: Plug It In, Then Fix It
sets.description: Ports, connectors, and display connections; setting up peripherals and sizing a UPS; and the six-step troubleshooting method.

intro.story: The Recursive Dragon has tangled every cable in the Guild hall and left the printers sulking. Ada the Chief Artificer will teach you which plug fits which port, and why a USB-C port that fits may still not carry your picture. Then she'll hand you the Guild's trouble tickets and the six steps that solve them.
objectives: Distinguish a port, a connector, and a standard, and compare USB, Thunderbolt, and Lightning
Compare wireless peripherals (Bluetooth, RF, and IR) and display connectors (VGA, DVI, HDMI, DisplayPort, and USB-C)
Choose a display connection by checking shape, signal, and speed, and tell mirroring from casting
Explain plug and play, set up common peripherals, and size a UPS
Apply the six-step troubleshooting method, and treat an AI's answer as a theory to test
